tldr: The authors propose a method that automatically reconstructs 3D environments, objects, and contact states in a physics simulator from everyday human activity captured by smart glasses. By optimizing whole-body motion adapted to the robot's morphology, it trains humanoid loco-manipulation VLA policies without using any real-robot teleoperation demonstrations.
hero_caption: Overall framework of E2S2H. From smart glasses RGB-D, head poses, and hand trajectories, it autonomously reconstructs the scene and target contact bands. Through whole-body motion adaptation that bridges morphological differences and reinforcement learning for contact correction, it generates synthetic robot-view images paired with action labels. Full-body VLAs can be learned without any real-robot demonstrations.
overview:
Teaching humanoid robots whole-body loco-manipulation (coordinating walking and manipulation) for household chores and practical work requires massive amounts of behavioral data. However, conventional imitation learning requires trained operators to control expensive physical robots in real time via teleoperation, making it extremely difficult to scale to new environments and tasks. Meanwhile, using egocentric video captured by smart glasses worn by humans is convenient, but poses fundamental challenges: lower-body motion is not captured, and directly copying human motion fails to produce feasible contacts due to differences in stature, arm reach, and hand morphology between humans and robots.

To tackle this, the authors developed Ego2Sim2Humanoid (E2S2H), a pipeline that automatically converts egocentric human recordings into physically verified whole-body robot training trajectories. In this approach, an LLM-based coding agent reconstructs 3D meshes and collision geometries of backgrounds and objects from video, and predicts target contact bands on manipulated objects. Furthermore, by combining bilevel stance optimization tailored to robot morphology with reinforcement learning (RL) contact correction in physics simulation, it derives dynamically feasible whole-body motion, including out-of-view actions. Rendering the reconstructed scene through the onboard robot camera along the optimized rollout yields perfectly synchronized image-action pairs.

In real-robot experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid, the model was trained without a single episode of real-robot teleoperated demonstrations. As a result, fine-tuning the 3-billion-parameter VLA model GR00T N1.7 achieved autonomous success rates of 45% on a task of walking to lift a bottle from a table, and 25% on walking to pick up a hat and wear it. This represents a significant step showing that anyone can scale humanoid training data directly from daily video without tying up physical robots.
contributions: Established an agentic real-to-sim pipeline that automatically reconstructs 3D collision shapes and textured visual meshes for environments and objects from everyday egocentric RGB-D video without prior scans or CAD models, while identifying target contact bands on objects.

Developed a humanoid whole-body motion adaptation method that integrates grasp planning on target contact bands and collision-free standing posture planning (bilevel optimization), rather than blindly following human hand trajectories.

Implemented a two-stage motion correction mechanism that kinematically blends visibility transitions as hands enter and exit camera view, and employs in-simulation reinforcement learning to physically realize out-of-view actions and object holding under gravity.

Demonstrated autonomous real-robot loco-manipulation on a Unitree G1 with zero real-robot demonstrations, generating perfectly synchronized robot-view images, proprioception, and verified action labels from optimized physics rollouts.

sections.heading: Can smart glasses overcome the bottleneck of teleoperation data collection?
sections.summary: Full-body humanoid VLA training requires action-labeled trajectory data, but real-robot teleoperation is prohibitively expensive. Egocentric video offers an accessible alternative, yet it misses lower-body motion, and human-robot embodiment mismatches break contact tasks if motion is simply copied.
sections.details:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for humanoid robots offer a promising path toward general-purpose intelligence. However, existing imitation learning pipelines rely heavily on trajectory data gathered by skilled operators teleoperating physical robots. Gathering data by operating real hardware for every task and environment simply cannot scale.

Human egocentric video is an attractive, robot-free source of demonstrations. However, smart glasses record only head motion and in-view hands, omitting the trunk and legs that support the body. Consequently, previous work was limited to pretraining hand poses, ultimately still requiring real-robot teleoperation data for full-body joint control.

An even thornier issue is the embodiment mismatch. Humans and humanoids differ in height, arm reach, and the number and layout of fingers. Directly retargeting human hand motions (joint angle conversion) onto a robot causes the robot fingers to swing through air or deeply penetrate objects, throwing them away without achieving meaningful contact.

This is the core insight: E2S2H reconstructs the entire virtual environment from smart glasses RGB-D data (real-to-sim). Through morphology-adapted motion planning and reinforcement learning (RL) in a physics simulator, it generates physically verified robot trajectories. Rendering views from the robot's perspective inside the simulator builds a trainable dataset from scratch without any real-robot demonstrations.

captions.F2: System architecture of E2S2H. From the egocentric video in the top row, it constructs a textured scene with object masks and simplified collision models. In the bottom row, the robot gaze trajectory (green) is generated from the human head trajectory (orange). After synthesizing whole-body walking outside the view, planning hand contacts inside the view, and refining in physics simulation, it outputs robot-view training data.

sections.heading: How does cross-embodiment retargeting lead up to this point?
sections.summary: While transferring motion from human or robot video is widely studied, prior work focused on fixed-base arms or oversimplified locomotion, ignoring physical contact validity and failing to achieve precise full-body loco-manipulation.
sections.details:
### Data transfer from other embodiments and egocentric views
Techniques generating robot motion from human video (such as Masquerade and Ego2Robot) have advanced rapidly. However, most focus on table-mounted robot arms. Methods that visually replace human arms with robot arms without simulating physical contact often produce commands that fail to touch objects, despite looking plausible. Prior humanoid loco-manipulation work like EgoHumanoid reduced lower-body motion to three discrete walking commands ("forward", "turn", etc.), without verifying physical grasp stability.

### Humanoid retargeting and contemporary work
Retargeting human motion capture to humanoids in simulation is common, but differences in proportions often cause failures in precise hand-contact phases. Contemporaneous studies (such as $\lambda_0$ based on HumanVerse, and KODA) either do not explicitly physically verify scene and object geometry, or still require co-training with real-robot teleoperated demonstrations on target tasks.

In short, E2S2H's key differentiator is reconstructing objects and environments as physical assets from everyday un-scanned video, fully realizing contacts and whole-body motions on freely moving objects in physics simulation, and achieving zero real-robot demonstrations.

sections.heading: How does raw egocentric video become physically verified training data?
sections.summary: E2S2H consists of four integrated steps: agentic 3D scene reconstruction, bilevel stance and grasp planning to absorb morphological differences, RL-based dynamic contact correction, and robot-perspective image rendering.
sections.details:
The input consists of calibrated RGB-D video, 6-DoF head poses, and in-view 3D hand landmarks captured by Meta Project Aria Gen 2 smart glasses. No torso or leg data is provided. The output is a tuple of robot-view image $I_i$, proprioception $s_i$, language instruction $\ell$, and action tokens $a_i$ (a 64-dimensional whole-body latent plus 14-dimensional dual-hand joint targets).

### III-A Agentic real-to-sim
Instead of pre-scanning environments with LiDAR, an LLM-based coding agent reconstructs the scene in 3D for each everyday episode. The agent fits planes to the floor ($z=0$) and support surfaces like tables, and tracks 6-DoF object poses via silhouette matching. It generates visual meshes via TSDF (Truncated Signed Distance Field) and completes unobserved backsides with geometric primitives like superellipsoids. Furthermore, it detects when and where human hands touch the object, automatically establishing target contact bands on object surfaces.

### III-B Motion adaptation
Projecting human head trajectories onto the floor forms the robot's base path, but humans and robots differ in height and reach. A bilevel optimization problem solves for reachable, collision-free standing postures $s\in\mathrm{SE}(2)$ along with pelvis and arm poses. Rather than copying human hand poses directly onto the robot hand (Unitree G1's 3-finger Dex3), a rule-based grasp planner runs against estimated contact bands to find feasible wrist poses and finger closures with proper pad contact. Generative models (Kimodo) synthesize lower-body locomotion and out-of-view arm motions.

### III-C & III-D Kinematic and RL dynamic motion correction
To avoid abrupt velocity spikes as hands enter camera view, hand trajectories are blended kinematically using a smooth fade function. However, this alone cannot guarantee that objects stay supported under gravity without dropping or destabilizing the robot. Thus, an RL tracking policy is trained in physics simulation. The agent designs semantic rewards to guide contact maintenance and transport goals. For tasks like wearing a hat where the object leaves camera view near the head, relative distance rewards between body links and the object allow the policy to reliably finish the phase in simulation.

### III-E Robot-view rendering and policy learning
Finally, images from the robot head camera are rendered along successful physics rollouts. The rendered frames reflect the robot's stature and show its own arms instead of human ones. Using only this synchronized dataset, the foundation model GR00T N1.7 (3B) is fine-tuned via behavioral cloning.

sections.heading: Can a humanoid really execute loco-manipulation without real-robot demonstrations?
sections.summary: Validated on a Unitree G1 across bottle lifting and hat wearing tasks. The grasp planner significantly reduced hand penetration, and real-robot evaluations achieved autonomous locomotion, grasping, and manipulation without any teleoperation data.
sections.details:
### Tasks and datasets
Captured human egocentric recordings cover two tasks: walking to lift a bottle on a table ("bottle lift", 219 episodes) and walking to pick up a hat and place it on the head ("hat wearing", 154 episodes). Participants wore Aria Gen 2 glasses and performed tasks naturally without external cameras or body trackers. After passing pipeline verification filters, 189 bottle and 59 hat episodes were retained for training. The hat task had higher attrition because hat brims are only millimeters thick, causing dropped-object failures in simulation if finger pinches were imperfect.

### Grasp planning efficacy and prior work comparison
Comparing the proposed grasp planner with a baseline directly copying human hand poses (Copied Palm) on the hat task, the proposed method cut median hand-link penetration depth into the object by more than half, from 1.8 cm to 0.8 cm. It also substantially reduced object slippage during grasping (translation dropped from 6.6 cm to 3.7 cm; rotation from 33.0 deg to 22.9 deg).

Compared to prior baselines EgoHumanoid and EgoHumanoid-V2, which stalled at path completion ratios around 0.5–0.6 and ended with hand-to-target distances over 70 cm (resulting in 0 successful grasps), E2S2H achieved a 0.9 path completion ratio, a median hand distance of 0.8 cm, and produced 57 valid grasps.

### Real-robot evaluation results
The fine-tuned GR00T N1.7 model was deployed on a physical Unitree G1 for 20 autonomous trials per task. In bottle lifting, it reached the table in 85% (17/20) and achieved a final success rate of 45% (9/20), never dropping the bottle once grasped. In hat wearing, it reached the table in 100% (20/20), succeeded in grasping in 40% (8/20), and reached 25% (5/20) final task success, including placing it out-of-view onto the head. Given zero real-robot teleoperated demonstrations, these results are remarkably strong.

captions.F5: Autonomous real-robot task execution on the Unitree G1. Bottle lifting is on the left, and hat wearing is on the right. Semi-transparent past frames are overlaid, illustrating smooth whole-body coordination from walking approach to table grasping, and transporting the hat onto the robot's head.

sections.heading: What are the remaining hurdles in sim-to-real transfer?
sections.summary: Key challenges include potential sim-to-real gaps for heavy objects due to guessing physical parameters from video, as well as an inability to handle highly deformable objects beyond rigid and articulated bodies.
sections.details:
The authors highlight several limitations:

- Physical dynamic parameters such as object mass, inertia tensors, and friction coefficients are inferred from video (priors). While RL robustness absorbs inaccuracies for lightweight everyday items, heavy or highly off-center objects may introduce problematic sim-to-real gaps.
- The real-to-sim representation is currently limited to rigid bodies, parametric shapes, and revolute joints. Tasks involving deformable cloth folding, bread cutting, or liquid pouring that undergo geometric and topological changes cannot yet be handled.

sections.heading: A major leap forward for scalable humanoid data collection
sections.summary: E2S2H demonstrates that physically verified full-body trajectories can be synthesized from daily egocentric video via physics simulation, enabling VLA training without real-robot demonstrations and opening a path to ubiquitous humanoid data scaling.
sections.details:
Smart glasses recordings are convenient, but capture only where someone looked and how in-view hands moved. By coupling contact band identification, morphology-adapted grasp and stance planning, physics-based RL refinement, and robot-perspective rendering, E2S2H successfully turns raw video into actionable, reliable robot training data.

This makes it possible to train loco-manipulation policies directly from everyday video without expensive humanoid hardware, expert teleoperators, or pre-scanned environments. It provides a powerful foundation for scaling humanoid behavioral data to internet-scale, everyday environments.

sections.heading: Appendix: Details of reconstruction algorithms and optimization
sections.summary: Details the formulation of agentic plane fitting, shape completion, bilevel stance and rule-based grasp optimization, as well as semantic reward designs for out-of-view manipulation phases.
sections.details:
### Real-to-sim geometry and contact band estimation
After verifying the geometric consistency of stereo depth maps, support planes (tables, etc.) and the floor are extracted via robust M-estimation. For textured object meshes, colors are baked from optimal viewpoints weighted by surface normals and camera distances. Unobserved back surfaces are closed using least-squares superellipsoid fitting. Target contact bands $\mathcal{R}_m$ are defined as local patches or bands projected onto object surfaces at the moment of human hand-object proximity and grasp.

### Bilevel stance planning and rule-based grasping
Stance optimization is formulated as a bilevel problem: an inner loop solves inverse kinematics (IK) honoring joint limits, while an outer loop enforces an obstacle clearance margin $d_{\text{s}}$. Grasp planning solves bounded least-squares optimization using MuJoCo signed distance fields between geoms. It constrains the thumb and index/middle pads to pinch opposite sides of the contact band, while keeping palm and forearm orientations within 12–15 degrees of the human demonstration.

### Motion blending and RL rewards
Over a 0.6-second fade window when hands enter camera view, smooth kinematic interpolation is applied using a cubic spline $\beta(u)=3u^2-2u^3$. In simulation RL, beyond joint torque smoothness and tracking terms, Gaussian kernel rewards $\kappa(e;\varsigma)=\exp(-\|e\|^2/\varsigma^2)$ penalize relative position and orientation errors between the object and target robot links (such as the head link in the hat task), enabling precise out-of-view completion.

takeaways: Directly copying human hand trajectories to a robot wrist fails due to stature and finger morphology differences; replanning grasps using target contact bands on the object is essential.
Humanoid loco-manipulation requires solving upper-body reach and collision-free foot placement simultaneously via bilevel stance optimization.
Blind spots of smart glasses (out-of-view manipulation and missing lower-body motion) can be resolved by combining generative motion models with in-simulation RL guided by relative body-link rewards.
Rendering robot-perspective imagery from physically verified simulation rollouts makes training real-robot VLAs entirely practical without a single teleoperated real-robot demonstration.
limitations: Object mass, friction, and center-of-mass are inferred from video priors, posing sim-to-real transfer risks for heavy or off-balance objects.
The framework assumes rigid bodies, simple parametric shapes, or revolute joints, meaning it cannot currently handle deformable objects like clothing or topological changes like cutting and pouring.
For millimeter-thin geometries like hat brims, grasp planning margins are extremely narrow, causing many episodes to be filtered out during physics simulation checks.
